MERCEDES-BENZ 280 SE 3.5 CABRIOLET

In the pantheon of postwar luxury automobiles, few models command the reverence, and admiration accorded the Mercedes-Benz W111-series Cabriolet, and none more so than the potent and lavishly appointed 280 SE 3.5. Introduced in late 1969, the 3.5-liter variant marked the ultimate evolution of the prestigious W111 platform, at once marrying Mercedes-Benz's storied engineering prowess with newfound V8 performance and subtle, old-world elegance.

Conceived at a time when Mercedes-Benz sought to reaffirm its leadership within the realm of open Grand Tourers, the 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet combined the sweeping, pillarless silhouette of the original Paul Bracq-penned design with significant mechanical advancements. At its heart lay the M116 V8: a single-overhead-cam, all-alloy motor of 3,499 cubic centimeters, breathing through sophisticated Bosch D-Jetronic electronic fuel injection. This combination yielded an exhilarating 200bhp, a figure that transformed the W111 Cabriolet from stately tourer to swift express, fully capable of sustained Autobahn velocities.

Hand-assembled in limited numbers at the legendary Sindelfingen works, the 3.5 Cabriolet was a singular accomplishment, blending robust German engineering with the finest materials available. The opulent interiors featured exotic wood veneers, hand-stitched leather, and finely chromed hardware—details emblematic of Mercedes-Benz's uncompromising standard of craftsmanship. Furthermore, the model's fully independent suspension and four-wheel disc brakes complemented the powerful V8, ensuring dynamic poise and refined composure on both sweeping highways and sinuous country roads.

The exclusivity of the 3.5 Cabriolet was defined not only by its performance or luxury, but also by its scarcity. Just 1,232 Cabriolets were produced between 1969 and 1971, and fewer still were delivered to original European specification. Today, their desirability persists, with discerning collectors coveting unrestored examples or those returned to as-new condition by the world's foremost specialists.

The 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet enjoys an exalted reputation amongst Mercedes-Benz connoisseurs, owing to its place as the final hand-built, open-top model of the classic era. It stands as Mercedes-Benz's swan song to a world before mass production altered the automotive landscape—a graceful, V8-powered masterwork embodying both the manufacturer's technical acumen and its dedication to understated elegance.

In period, the 3.5 Cabriolet was the preferred conveyance of captains of industry, film stars, and heads of state, offering unparalleled comfort and performance in equal measure. Its effortless road manners, ample power reserves, and whisper-quiet operation set a benchmark that rivals and successors would struggle to attain.

Further elevating its appeal is the car's ability to blend discreet luxury with subtle aggression. At a glance, the casual observer might miss the discreet "3.5" badging and low, wide grille—further emphasizing its status as a sophisticated grand tourer for those who value substance over ostentation.

Today, the W111 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet stands at the zenith of postwar Mercedes-Benz collector interest, cherished for its rarity, integrity, and fully realized synthesis of performance and grace. The finest examples—those retaining their original mechanicals and finished in compelling color schemes—are considered blue-chip investments within the international collector community.


THE CAR OFFERED

Stunning in provenance and presentation, this 1971 Mercedes-Benz 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet, chassis 11102712000587, represents the paragon of W111 open-air motoring.

Delivered new to its first owner, Joachim H. Lindner of Gersthofen, Augsburg, the car commenced its journey in the heart of Germany, where it would be meticulously maintained and successively registered within Bavaria. Its lineage is substantiated by an unbroken chain of German registration documents, including the original Kraftfahrzeugbrief and Abmeldebescheinigung, underscoring its authentic European specification and confirming its status as a desirable EU-market car.

Significantly, this 280 SE 3.5 preserves its factory-issued engine, number 116980-12-000412, as well as its original automatic transmission, affirming the all-important "matching numbers" pedigree so valued among Mercedes-Benz collectors. Such authenticity is further supported by the car's original color scheme—Anthrazitgrau Metallic over Tan leather—an extraordinarily rare and elegant pairing that amplifies the car's enduring visual appeal.

A comprehensive, frame-off restoration was executed by renowned marque authority Arthur Bechtel of Germany, a name synonymous with the highest standards of Mercedes-Benz craftsmanship. Throughout the process, Mr. Bechtel and his atelier adhered unwaveringly to original specifications, utilizing period-correct materials and techniques. Known for their award-winning work particularly on the famed 300SL Gullwing and Roadster, Bechtel's signature is evident in every detail of this exceptional Cabriolet, from the subtle luster of its anthracite-gray finish to the impeccable hand-stitched tan hides gracing the interior.

The car's restoration was commissioned to elevate every mechanical and cosmetic aspect to concours-standard, while ensuring functional integrity commensurate with modern collector expectations. The result is a 280 SE 3.5 that performs as impressively as it presents, benefitting from a rebuilt Bosch D-Jetronic system, overhauled suspension, and factory-correct ignition and instrumentation. The restoration's documentation, including a commercial invoice for $312,000 from Bechtel Motorcompany GmbH, accompanies the car, affirming both the investment in its rebirth and the caliber of workmanship applied throughout.

The car has traveled a mere 768 miles since the completion of its restoration, positioning it as a virtually fresh and unspoiled example—ideal for concours exhibition or gentle touring. The integrity of its presentation is further enhanced by its historic registration status (plate MB FM4 H) and inclusion of original chassis documentation, reaffirming its continuous German provenance prior to its recent exportation to Canada in May 2024.

This 1971 Mercedes-Benz 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet offers an unparalleled opportunity to acquire one of the most sought-after open Mercedes-Benz models of the postwar era, endowed with pedigree, provenance, and peerless presentation. For the discerning collector seeking an investment-grade example restored by one of Germany's preeminent specialists, chassis 11102712000587 presents itself as a true exemplar—ready for immediate enjoyment, prestigious display, or inclusion within the world's most significant automotive collections.

THE F12TDF

Introduced to the motoring public at the 2102 Geneva Motor Show, the Ferrari F12 replaced the 599 family of front-engined Gran Turismos. Ferrari's gorgeous new berlinetta was soon garnering critical accolades, being voted 'Supercar of the Year 2012' by Top Gear magazine, and in 2014 receiving the coveted 'Premio Compasso d'Oro ADI', one of the world's oldest and most prestigious design awards.

It is an oft-stated cliché that 'the heart of every Ferrari is its engine', and the F12's 6.3-liter, 65-degree, normally aspirated V12 is acknowledged as one of the finest ever, winning the 'Best Performance' and 'Best Engine above 4.0 liters' categories in the 2013 'International Engine of the Year Awards'. With 730bhp on tap, this class-leading power unit - one of the most powerful every installed in a Ferrari road car – delivers stupendous performance, propelling the F12 to 100km/h (62mph) in 3.1 seconds on its way to a top speed of 211mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, the F12 proved to be 3.5 seconds quicker that the preceding 599 GTB and 2.0 seconds quicker than the mid-engined Enzo; even the hardcore 599 GTO was slower.

But these days even a supercar has to make the odd concession in the interests of fuel economy, and with this in mind the F12 incorporated Ferrari's HELE stop/start system that reduces consumption when idling. Paddle shifters mounted on the steering wheel – an innovation pioneered by Ferrari in Formula 1 - had long been a feature of the Maranello marque's road cars, and the F12's controlled a seven-speed dual-clutch semi-automatic transmission. Stability, traction control, suspension, and other settings were also controlled from the F12's steering wheel, while improved carbon-ceramic brakes helped keep things in check.

The engine/transmission package was mounted in an aluminum spaceframe chassis - developed by Ferrari's close neighbors and long-time collaborators, Carrozzeria Scaglietti – that represented significant gains in rigidity and weight reduction when compared with the preceding 599 GTB. As one would expect of a modern-day Ferrari supercar, the F12 came with the latest in driver aids as standard: ABS, SCM-E magnetorheological suspension, electronic limited-slip differential, ESP Premium stability control, and F1-Trac traction control.

Styled by the Ferrari Styling Centre and Carrozzeria Pininfarina, the F12's voluptuous body restated the traditional 'long bonnet, small cabin, short tail' look in a manner suggesting muscular horsepower while retaining all the elegance associated with the Italian coachbuilder's work for Maranello. A significant aerodynamic development was the 'Aero Bridge': an under-body air channel running from front to rear that increased down force while exerting less drag than an external wing. 'Active Brake Cooling' ducts had been adopted for the same reason; opening only when the brakes required cooling while remaining closed at other times to reduce aerodynamic drag. The result was a remarkably low drag coefficient of only 0.299. Based on that of the Ferrari FF, the 'Frau leather' interior featured aluminum, Alutex, and carbon fiber trim. The F12's optional accessories were extensive, though pricey: who would have thought that a carbon fiber cup holder could cost over €2,000?

In October 2015, Ferrari announced a limited-edition variant, the F12tdf, its nomenclature referencing a competition variant of the 250 GT, so named following the latter's many victories in the Tour de France Automobile in the late 1950s/early 1960s. Like its illustrious predecessor, the F12tdf was a lightweight, track-focused model aimed at wealthy connoisseurs and gentleman racers; only 799 were built during the 2016 and 2017 seasons.


THE CAR OFFERED

Greatness does not spring forth without effort and just as children do not erupt fully grown from their parents like Athena, great cars require time, effort, and honing to reach perfection. As Ferrari was taking its F12 to the next level with the track-focused F12tdf, this development prototype was used to help the model reach its zenith. Outside of the numbered run of 799 examples (including the one offered in this auction), this European market F12 Berlinetta is finished in Nero with white rondels on the doors and hood and trimmed inside in Nero leather. Used to develop the F12tdf starting in mid-2014, beneath the standard F12 hood is a prototype example of the firebreather that would power the production model.

Development mules and prototypes are often scraped after their useful life as guinea pigs is over—but Ferrari offers these unique specimens to their top clients to round out their collections. As a development prototype, the car has been labeled as "Not Street Legal" and as such cannot be registered or titled. Showing about 20,000 miles, it is the perfect diamond in the rough to round out a Ferrari collection.

NISSAN SKYLINE R32 GT-R

It was in 1957 that the 'Skyline' name was introduced by the Japanese manufacturer Prince, to denote its luxury model. After the company merged with Nissan in 1967, the moniker jumped ship to the Nissan brand with 1968's C10 variant. Its new custodian regarded it as a performance badge, with the first GT-R appearing in 1969. As the flagship Skyline, it focused on delivering speed and style.

Routinely voted by the classic car magazines as one of the greatest Japanese cars of all time, Nissan's high-tech Skyline GT-R burst onto the motoring scene in 1989 to universal acclaim. Built specifically to contest Group A, the original R32 GT-R Skyline dominated the Australian racing scene, earning the nickname 'Godzilla' and ultimately, banishment from the ATCC. Debuting at Mallala in June 1990, the R32 race program was run by Gibson Motorsport and from the outset it was clear the car had the potential to be a race winner but it wasn't until 1991 that everything came together for the team and drivers Jim Richards and Mark Skaife crushed the opposition, including a win at the all-important Bathurst enduro. Despite increased minimum weight and reduced boost bar for 1992, the Skyline continued its winning ways, famously scoring a repeat win at Bathurst in the toughest condition - and a hostile reception from the crowd when Richards and Skaife took the podium.

In road going form, the R32 was powered by a twin-turbo RB26DETT in-line six allied with a sophisticated 4WD system and HICAS all-wheel steering, the R32 was a devastating road car. On paper, these cars were stated to produce 276hp, however these were usually underrated numbers to please the limiting laws in Japan. Unofficially the Skyline held the lap record on the legendary Nürburgring Nordschleife.


THE CAR OFFERED

When legendary tuner Kazuhiko "Smokey" Nagata of Top-Secret Japan applies his expertise, the results are nothing short of extraordinary—and this 1993 Skyline R32 GT-R is a perfect example. This project started as a carefully picked chassis, a great basis with low mileage and excellent condition, perfect for a well-suited performance build. Built for both circuit racing and canyon driving, it features a bored and stroked 2.8L version of the legendary 2.6L RB26 N1 engine, with ported and polished head, twin enlarged turbochargers, fortified rods, pistons and cams, and a host of other performance enhancements that unleash serious horsepower. This Skyline also received a custom calibrated standalone HKS ECU to control the host of engine upgrades to this impressive powerplant.

The 5-speed manual transmission has been rebuilt with an aftermarket clutch to handle the extra output, while the chassis has been fine-tuned with an AP Racing big brake kit, custom HKS suspension, anti-roll bars, and stylish Top Secret spec Italian built OZ Racing 10-spoke wheels wrapped in ultra-grippy, Bridgestone low-profile tires.

Most custom builds from performance tuning shop Top Secret Japan are finished in their signature gold livery, where this version stays extremely unique as one of their rare examples, known as 'Yuki Chan' finished in white with black lower-sill striping. The right-hand drive cabin is race-ready yet refined, featuring factory bucket seats, well-appointed steering wheel and shifter, custom glove-compartment gauges, and a full roll cage. This example of the legendary Skyline legacy, showing very low mileage of under 40,000 kilometers on the clock, is a hard-to-find example of the forbidden JDM fruit found in the United States. Rare, purposeful, and thrilling to drive, this Skyline R32 GT-R represents a truly exceptional piece of Japanese tuning history and is arguably worthy of supercar status.

THE PORSCHE 964 CARRERA RS

'What the RS has done is take the technical brilliance of the latest Carreras and put back the missing excitement of some earlier, less pampering generations.' – Brian Laban, Performance Car magazine.

Evoking memories of the legendary 2.7 and 3.0-liter RS and RSR 'homologation specials' of the 1970s, in 1991 Porsche introduced the Type 964 Carrera RS. A lightweight variant like its illustrious forebears, the beautiful newcomer was based on the 'Carrera Cup' competition car and sold in Europe only, though there was a lower-specification 'RS America' for the United States market. There was also a Touring version that kept most of the road equipment fitted to the standard Carrera.

The Carrera RS retained the 3.6-liter engine, albeit boosted in maximum output to 260bhp and equipped with a lightened flywheel for improved response. The G50/10 five-speed transmission featured closer ratios, an asymmetrical limited-slip differential, and steel synchromesh, while the suspension was lowered and stiffened. The 0-100km/h time dropped to 5.4 seconds, and the Carrera RS had a top speed of 260km/h.

The interior was stripped out completely and the power steering, power windows and seats, rear seats, air conditioning, cruise control, sound deadening material, and stereo system removed. Two lightweight racing bucket seats were fitted instead. The front bonnet was made of aluminum and parts of the chassis were seam welded, while the side windows were made from thinner and lighter glass. Rounding off this radical exercise in weight reduction, the Carrera RS was equipped with 17" Cup magnesium wheels. The result was a total weight saving of around 150kg compared to the Carrera 2, transforming the RS into a faster, more agile, and more responsive car.

Brian Laban found that any feeling of remoteness or soft touch had gone completely and reckoned that the controls never felt more solid or precise. In his opinion the Porsche could not be faulted, the verdict being that the Carrera RS was 'exactly what a performance car should be'.


THE CAR OFFERED

Manufactured new in April of 1992, this 964 Carrera RS coupé was delivered in iconic Guards Red over black/pearl gray multi tone interior; an always favored Porsche color combination. This RS was made to Japanese specification and sold new in the Land of the Rising Sun; later being imported to the United States in 2024.

As it sits today, this beautifully presented Carrera RS has covered less than 52,350 kilometers (approximately 32,528 miles) from new at the time of cataloguing and presents in great condition. The level of care given to this car is seen throughout, from the interior to the engine compartment and under the front bonnet, which appears seemingly untouched. The undercarriage is very well presented and clean, as are the suspension components and bottom of the engine bay.

The stripped-down interior fitted with factory Recaro bucket seats and minimally equipped door cards, with tether strap door releases, shows the effort kept in creating a competition focused RS for the road by offering only the essentials for a pure driver focused experience. Mirroring its exterior, the cabin presents in excellent condition, only showing minimal wear on the driver's seat bolster, and is otherwise beautifully well kept. The red seat belts are a nice touch to match with the Guards Red livery. The car is accompanied by its owner's manual, tool kit, service records, export documents, and a Porsche Production Specification Certificate.

It is often argued that the best Porsches are the lightweight, track-ready variants, and many would argue that the Carrera RS is the most exciting and analog of the 964 generation. Being offered today, this low-mileage example will not disappoint, providing a pure, unhindered driving experience. With the foundation set in Porsche's legendary motorsports history, this competition derived Carrera RS continues to increase in collectability as low mileage examples such as this are becoming increasingly harder to find.

THE KOENIGSEGG REGERA

Unveiled at the 2015 Geneva Motor Show and produced between 2016 and 2022, the Koenigsegg Regera (Swedish for 'Koenigsegg Reigns') is a landmark in automotive engineering, blending staggering performance with unprecedented luxury. The brainchild of Christian von Koenigsegg and developed entirely in-house at the company's Ängelholm facility in Sweden, the Regera was conceived as a hybrid hypercar with grand touring comfort — a one-car solution for collectors seeking both track-level potency and refinement for long-distance driving.

The Regera was offered in a strictly limited production run of just 80 units, all of which were pre-sold and every Regera was hand-built to bespoke specifications, ensuring each is unique.

The Regera is powered by a 5.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine with a redline at 8,250rpm, paired with three electric motors (two at the rear wheels and one on the crankshaft), producing a combined output of 1,500bhp and 2,000 Nm of torque at 4,100rpm. The car features the Koenigsegg Direct Drive (KDD) system — a patented, single-speed gear solution that couples the engine and the electric motors to the rear axle, replacing the traditional multi-speed transmission, reducing weight and drivetrain drag, with rocket-launch acceleration. As a result, the car is capable of accelerating from 0–100 km/h in 2.8 seconds, from 0–300 km/h in under 10 seconds and 0-400 km/h in just over 20 seconds – a world-record number. Yet, despite this savage performance, the Regera also offers electric-only propulsion for silent low-speed urban use.

The carbon fiber monocoque chassis and body are wrapped in sculpted carbon panels, with active aerodynamics including an automatically deploying rear wing and hydraulically adjustable ride height and damping, inducing a total down force of 450 kg at 250 km/h. This two-door two-seater has a removable structural hardtop stowable under the front hood and lightweight anti-roll bars front and rear. For driving in changeable conditions or commuting to the track, the car offers the proprietary Koenigsegg Electronic Stability Control System with four setting for Comfort, Wet/Snow, Sport and Track, underlining the vehicle's versatility. Another of the Regera's crowning glories is its bespoke titanium exhaust system, developed with Akrapovic.

The cockpit is finished to an extraordinary standard, boasting contrasting black and white stitched leather on the highly stylized memory foam seats and facias, ambient lighting and an intuitive infotainment system with Apple CarPlay and Wi-Fi connectivity. Koenigsegg's "Autoskin" system allows for remote-activated doors and hood and the bird's eye view parking assist with all round sensors makes parking a dream.


THE CAR OFFERED

This 2019 Regera is a heavily optioned example with over $1,000,000 in extras including in excess of $170,000 in exterior options such as 1 of 1 "One Shade Darker Candy Apple Red" paint with numerous exposed carbon fiber details, $285,000 for the Ghost package, $250,000 for the Environmental Power Upgrade, $57,000 for Tresex AirCore carbon fiber wheels, over $70,000 in bespoke interior options including Desiato Burgundy and Black quilted leather trim and numerous carbon fiber details, and $175,000 for the extended 5-year warranty (since expired). Additionally included is the unique Autoskin feature allowing the owner to open the doors, hood, and engine compartment with a touch of the buttons on the car's key/remote. The total MSRP was $3,241,000 as documented by a copy of the build sheet.

Sold new through Manhattan Motorcars in May of 2020, and bestowed the name "Elegua" – the deity of roads in a variety of African religious traditions – this example has been driven under 3,100 miles in the past six years. Regularly serviced throughout the years, the most recent record is from the end of February.

The unique machine in 1 of 1 spec and 1 of only 5 with both the Ghost Package and Environmental Power Upgrade is sure to excite. The Regera is not merely a track-day monster — it is a hyper-GT for the connoisseur, offering a uniquely serene driving experience, even at tremendous speed. With luggage space, comfort, and ease-of-use engineered into its design, the Regera is ideal for collectors seeking both road usability and exceptional performance pedigree. Reigning supreme in its cohort of hybrid hypercars and with its production now concluded, opportunities to own the Regera are exceedingly rare. This example represents the zenith of Koenigsegg's artistry: an engineering tour de force, limited in number, limitless in ambition.

THE McLAREN P1

Released in 1993, the McLaren F1 redefined what a supercar is and quickly made its mark as one the of the most impressive cars ever built. To this day the F1 evokes emotion difficult to express on a page. In 2013, 20 years later, McLaren turned back to its legendary creation but this time as inspiration for the world's first hybrid Supercar. Determined to revolutionize the Supercar market again, McLaren engineers used a 3.8-liter DOHC twin-turbocharged and intercooled V8 mated with an AC permanent-magnet synchronous electric motor to generate 903bhp. This stunning piece of engineering is mated to a carbon fiber MonoCage. It serves as the passenger compartment, safety cell, and the chassis' major structural component. The entire MonoCage, including roof and integrated battery compartment, weighs just 90kg!

The bodywork has been 'shrink-wrapped' over the mechanical hard points, and the cockpit has been placed at the exact center of the chassis. Helping keep the stunning powertrain tight to the road are active aerodynamic systems, which reduce drag and maximize downforce. The most impressive of which is the RCC (Race Active Chassis Control) system that provides unprecedented chassis adjustability through independent hydro-pneumatic control of spring rate and damping at each wheel. Another active aerodynamic feature are the movable front and rear wings that can produce a peak of 600kg of downforce in Race mode. All of these features add up to propel the P1 from 0-60mph in 2.7 seconds, and to 100mph in 5.1 seconds, and can achieve a top speed of 217mph.

This outstanding performance requires equally special brakes, and the P1 has those as well. Equipped with four-wheel carbon ceramic brakes with six-piston front calipers and four-piston rears, the P1 discs can absorb 50 percent more energy than conventional ceramic brakes. The P1 is also furnished with Brake Steer – a feature now banned in F1 for providing too much of an advantage – the system applies brake force to the inner wheel upon entry to a fast corner to bring the car's nose tighter to the apex. Upon exiting the corner, the same wheel is trimmed, pushing the torque to the outer wheel for increased traction while accelerating. In describing his road test, Daniel Pund of Car and Driver wrote, "It feels lithe and alert and well-mannered and entirely crackle-worthy. It is every bit as great to drive as you might hope it to be."

Hand-built to custom order at McLaren's Woking, England based state of the art and laboratory-like facilities, the P1 stems from a company deep-rooted in motor sport and performance automotive engineering. The company, the namesake of legendary racing driver Bruce McLaren, has been run for the past three decades by Ron Dennis, another motor sport great.

A synthesis of space age and Formula One technology, The P1 is a true modern automotive masterpiece of inspired design and engineering supremacy. Absolutely vicious acceleration with superb handling and braking deliver an exhilarating on-track experience, while remaining remarkably usable on the road.

Many will agree, that the P1 is the ultimate supercar of today and possibly tomorrow.


THE CAR OFFERED

Offered here is P1 number 209 of the total 375 car production-run, of which just about 150 examples were built for the US market like this car. Originally retailed through McLaren of Philadelphia, its first owner was a true enthusiast who specially commissioned the car in a unique Professor 2 Blue exterior shade with specially molded carbon fiber seats trimmed with red Daytona-style leather. An exhaustive commissioning process, nearly $140,000 in McLaren Special Operation options were selected. Retaining the car for two years, it set a world record when it was sold in 2017 to its next owner. Five years hence, the P1 would trade hands again entering the collection of its third owner.

It was in this ownership that this already spectacularly unique P1 was made even more special. Only ever offered as a coupe, the wizards at McLaren specialists Lanzante Limited set out to create an open-top iteration of the P1. Developed in collaboration with the P1's original designer, Paul Howse, the conversion preserves the P1's "organic fluidity" while introducing a pair of striking carbon fiber buttresses that house newly engineered air intakes to feed the twin-turbochargers. Despite the removal of the roof, the P1 Spider maintains its formidable structural integrity through Lanzante's meticulous chassis reinforcement. Brilliantly executed, the finished product looks as if it had emerged from the factory at Woking. A mere five examples were completed, each at a price of nearly double that of a P1 Coupe.

This P1 was the second Spider produced, s/n 209 is now trimmed in historic Gulf racing colors with an interior retrimmed in white, weather resistant SuperFabric UV-treated leather with Gulf accents. Driven fewer than 200 miles since Lanzante completed its Spider conversion and now showing under 3,000 miles from new, it is complete with two Gulf colored keys, a Lanzante build book, and the factory charging system.

An instant collector car, all 375 examples of the now legendary P1 are already sought after machines and this one-of-five P1 Spider by Lanzante is an order of magnitude more collectible.

THE ASTON MARTIN DB AR1

The early 2000s marked a period of bold reinvention for Aston Martin, as the iconic British marque sought not only to modernize its range but also to celebrate its rich tradition of bespoke, coach built excellence. Nowhere was this dual pursuit of innovation and heritage more exquisitely expressed than in the Aston Martin DB AR1—a limited production open-top grand tourer sculpted by the legendary Italian coachbuilder Zagato. Revealed to acclaim at the 2003 Los Angeles Auto Show, the DB AR1 (American Roadster 1) stands as a rarefied celebration of transcontinental luxury and performance, limited in production to just 99 examples, each tailored for discerning collectors and connoisseurs.

The DB AR1 is rooted in the mechanical underpinnings of the acclaimed DB7 Vantage Volante, sharing the model's robust aluminum-intensive chassis, yet dramatically reimagined in form and finish by Zagato's Milanese artisans. Its fluid lines, distinctive double-bubble tonneau fairings, and signature elliptical grille evoke a lineage of collaboration between Aston Martin and Zagato that traces back to the celebrated DB4 GT Zagato of the early 1960s. The unyielding commitment to open-air motoring is emphasized by the AR1's pure roadster configuration—eschewing even the fitment of a fixed roof or convertible top, affirming the car's devotion to spirited, fair-weather touring.

At the heart of the DB AR1 lies Aston Martin's formidable 5.9-liter V12, a 48-valve, quad-cam masterpiece assembled by hand at the company's Newport Pagnell works. Delivering 435 bhp at 6,000 rpm and paired in the AR1 with a six-speed manual transmission, the engine endows the car with effortless pace, resonant acoustics, and the distinguished authority expected of the marque. Performance is brisk and refined, with the roadster surging from rest to 60 mph in under five seconds, underscored by a supple independent suspension and responsive four-wheel disc brakes.

Luxury commensurate with the DB AR1's exclusivity is ever-present, from the bespoke Claret hides enveloping the cockpit to the carefully selected trim materials and lavishly appointed instrument panel. Each example was generously optioned and delivered with a suite of distinguishing accoutrements, further enhancing its status among contemporary collectables.

The rarity and handcrafted nature of the DB AR1, together with its provenance as a product of Zagato's fabled carrozzeria, imbues each car with tremendous collector appeal. Surviving examples—particularly those in unrestored, low-mileage, and well-documented condition—command especial esteem among aficionados who appreciate the blend of technical prowess, coach-built artistry, and total exclusivity.

More than two decades after its launch, the DB AR1 endures as an enduring emblem of Anglo-Italian collaboration—a car of singular narrative and presence, at once a contemporary grand tourer and a future heirloom of marque lore.

Conceived as a singular expression of Anglo-Italian artistry and roadster purity, the DB AR1 delivers a dynamic experience rooted in its formidable 5.9-liter, 48-valve, front-mounted V12—among the great engines of its era and a cornerstone of Aston Martin's modern resurgence. The six-speed manual transmission, seldom encountered elsewhere in the AR1, further elevates the driving engagement and collectability of this example.

Offered with a full suite of period-correct accessories and comprehensive service history, this is an exceptional candidate for the discerning collector seeking a reference-quality DB AR1. Its blend of Zagato coachbuilding, technical sophistication, and preserved authenticity assures its place as a centerpiece in any world-class collection of modern classics.

The McLaren 765LT Coupe represents the ultimate evolution of the Super Series, a lineage that began with the groundbreaking 12C and matured through the 650S and 720S. However, the LT—or "Longtail"—moniker elevates this machine beyond mere iteration, placing it within an elite sub-brand of McLaren history that traces its spiritual roots back to the F1 GTR of the 1990s. The 765LT is the result of a rigorous engineering philosophy that prioritizes mechanical purity, driver engagement, and weight reduction over all else. By shedding 80kg from the already lightweight 720S, McLaren engineers utilized advanced carbon fiber technologies and a titanium exhaust system to achieve a power-to-weight ratio that rivals most hypercars. The importance of the 765LT lies in its role as the final, most visceral expression of McLaren's non-hybrid internal combustion era. Its 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8, producing 755bhp, is tuned for a level of ferocity that marks a distinct departure from the clinical efficiency of its predecessors. This model introduced more aggressive aerodynamics, featuring a prominent active rear wing and a lengthened silhouette that provides 25% more downforce, ensuring the car remains glued to the tarmac at speeds exceeding 200 mph. Beyond the statistics, the 765LT serves as a cultural benchmark for the brand, embodying the transition from a purely data-driven pursuit of speed to a more emotive, sensory-focused driving experience. As global regulations shift toward electrification, the 765LT stands as a monumental bookend to a decade of internal combustion mastery, securing its place as a definitive modern classic. It is not just a faster car; it is the culmination of everything McLaren learned during its rapid ascent to the top of the supercar hierarchy, offered in a strictly limited run of 765 units that ensures its enduring exclusivity and significance.

THE DINO 246 GTS

In the vibrant tapestry of Ferrari history, the Dino occupies an especially prized and lyrical niche. Conceived in honor of Enzo Ferrari's late son, Alfredo "Dino" Ferrari, the 246 series marked a significant departure for Maranello. It was the marque's first mid-engined, six-cylinder road car—an eloquent bridge between motorsport and the open road, named not Ferrari, but simply "Dino," suggesting both reverence and a sense of evolving identity.

Launched in 1969, the Dino 246 GT captured the imagination of enthusiasts and the public alike, blending Ferrari's commitment to mechanical excellence with shapely, Pininfarina-penned coachwork by Scaglietti. The 246 GTS, unveiled in 1972, built on this legacy, introducing a targa-style variant that added a new dimension of open-air motoring while preserving the coupe's distinctive proportions. With its removable roof panel, "GTS" offered an intoxicating union of Supercar drama and the sunshine of la dolce vita.

At the heart of every 246 beats the revered 2.4-liter dual overhead cam V-6, derived from Formula 2 roots and characterized by responsive power delivery and thrilling aural character. Triple Weber 40 DCNF carburetors, alongside a 5-speed dogleg manual transmission, imbue the car with an unmistakable sense of mechanical connection—supple and tractable enough for daily use, but transcendent at the redline.

Chassis sophistication was equally advanced, with an all-independent suspension and four-wheel disc brakes—features that gave the Dino surprising agility and composure. Lightweight and balanced, the 246 quickly earned a reputation for purity of handling; its steering and throttle response remain benchmarks for driver involvement.

The Dino's coachwork, with its curvaceous flanks and delicate details, is widely regarded as one of Pininfarina's masterpieces. Interior appointments were no less considered—the laid-back driving position, aircraft-inspired Veglia instrumentation, and available Daytona-style seats made each journey an event.

Originally intended to challenge rivals like the Porsche 911S, the Dino instead carved out its own cult following. Only 1,274 GTS models were built between 1972 and 1974; a mere fraction were finished in rare metallic and special-order paint schemes (like Marrone Dino Metallizzato), marking such examples as true connoisseur's prizes today.

In the decades since production ended, the Dino's reputation has matured immeasurably. Where it was once an "almost-Ferrari," it is now recognized as one of the marque's most poetic and influential creations. The GTS models, in particular, capture an era of playful, unrestrained artistry in both mechanical design and visual language.

THE LaFERRARI

"We chose to call this model LaFerrari because it is the finest expression of our company's unique, unparalleled engineering and design know-how, including that acquired in Formula One."

This is how chairman Luca di Montezemolo summarized the successor to the Enzo when it was launched at the Geneva Salon, in March 2013. He would later state that the complete run sold out at the show, with 700 requests for the planned 499 car production run.

It is hard not to consider this as both the zenith and the grand finale of his amazing two decades at the helm of the world's greatest sportscar brand. The following fall he would announce that he would step down as its chairman.

In the decade that had passed since the Enzo started to be delivered, Formula 1 regulations had changed dramatically, technology had adapted, become more 'green' even... As Montezemolo stated, everything they had learned now went into the new car.

Of course, in many respects it was obvious that a decade of technology would bring the car light years ahead of its predecessor, but it was a carefully thought-out process that arrived at the finished article.

Powered by a normally aspirated 6.3 liter V12, which could put out some 800bhp, the internal combustion engine was no longer the sole source of energy/power. The 'green' aspect was the arrival of the Hybrid Kinetic Energy Recovery System, which had appeared on F1 cars in 2009. As on those they were determined would provide not only the reductions in emissions and fuel consumption but also provide the performance boost that was seen on the racetrack in their single seaters.

First off, the new car had to be lighter, the goal being a saving of nearly 20%. This was something of a tightrope to walk as they knew they knew the KERS technology was a weight gain. The designers elected to make the car some 900mm shorter than an Enzo, and wherever possible use the same build techniques and ultra-lightweight materials as they were in the contemporary racecars. Every aspect was looked at, details such as a complete reworking of how the seating was built, now the driver would effectively sit on upholstery which was fixed to the cockpit and the pedals and steering wheel would simply allow for driver adjustment, the seat structures themselves were eliminated. Reductions in the thickness of the carbon fiber body panels and even using lighter paint itself bought 17kg.

The hybrid KERS chosen was itself subjected to rigorous refinement to shave some 50kg off its expected 200kg added weight. The effect of the system they created is nothing short of staggering in terms of performance, long term suppliers Magneti Marelli providing two electric power units to separately power the wheels and ancillaries.

The electric motor's 120 kilowatts, which equate to roughly 163hp work in harmony with the V12's 800 hp, providing unheard of acceleration at lower speeds and protecting the upper rev bands for outright speed, a mind numbing 9,250 rpm redline point.

The resulting car was nothing short of spectacular, staying true its bloodline, with two-wheel drive configuration. Its power combination driving through a seven speed dual clutch transmission, provided lightning quick acceleration, with the following remarkable set of figures:

0-62mph (100kph) in less than 3 seconds
0-124mph (200kph) in less than 7 seconds
0-186mph (300kph) in less than 15 seconds

The manufacturer would report a time of 1 minute 19.70 seconds around its Fiorano Test Track, faster than any car they had ever produced, and some 5 seconds faster than an Enzo! While a quarter mile at 9.7 seconds put it faster than both the 918 Porsche and Bugatti Veyron Super Sport.

And then there's the aesthetics to consider. Each time Ferrari has elected to produce the ultimate sports car of its day, they have produced something totally out of the box, fresh, innovative, striking and individual. As nothing had prepared the world for the looks of an F40 or Enzo, the statement made by LaFerrari had to match that. They chose to work in house, a rare step aside from their relationship with Pininfarina, Ferrari Centro Stile's Flavio Manzoni being responsible for the exquisite design, which is both striking and modern yet gives nods to the brand heritage.

Road and Track's Larry Webster had the privilege of driving a La Ferrari just over a year ago, in Maranello on the day after Sebastian Vettel had secured a popular win for the Tifosi at Hungary, a great day to be at the Ferrari homebase.

It's a fascinating review of this incredible sports car, begun with "I pressed the starter button, lighting off the V12. A flock of birds evacuated a nearby tree." The performance clearly blew him away... "What happened next is cloudy. Launch mode (stability control off, hold the brake, press the launch button, floor the gas, and release the brake) brings engine revs to about 3000 and aggressively engages the clutch. The wheels spun for maybe half a second before the computer upshifted to second. I remember watching the speedometer increase in 10-mph gulps, a blur of flashing digits. Every upshift banged my head on the seat. The V12 sounded as if it was always pegged at redline. A bridge that had seemed a long way off suddenly appeared overhead."

He concludes "There's a lot of talk nowadays about how civilized sports cars have become. How modern tires and electronic systems have insulated drivers from the delicate touch that was once required. The LaFerrari stands that notion on end. To be quick, it demands a style that's both aggressive and delicate. An amazing amount of speed is available to even modestly skilled drivers, and the electronics provide a safety net. But only the truly skilled can deploy all it offers.

Every exotic car should have a tinge of risk. It's impossible to quantify—a VBOX can't measure it. But take the LaFerrari where it wants to go, for those extra few seconds, and the fangs come out. And that's exactly how it should be."

It's hard to argue with such sentiments...

Few songs are more emblematic of the sports car hobby than Sammy Hagar's iconic 1984 hit single "I Can't Drive 55". But far beyond just that, Hagar has been a fixture of the rock and roll scene as a soloist and the second lead singer of Van Halen. As if being musical royalty and a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee, Hagar has been a successful restaurateur as well as launching multiple successful spirits brands including Cabo Wabo tequila and Santa tequila. And coming as no surprise to anyone, Hagar is also a dyed in the wool car enthusiast.

This one-of-kind LaFerrari was ordered new by the Red Rocker himself and carefully specified to his rather fine tastes. Finished in Avorio (Ivory) with Tetto Nero DS accent trim, the color was picked after seeing how well it suited Ferraris of the 1960s. Inside, the seats are trimmed in matching Avorio Alcantara with black trim accents and optional gloss carbon fiber trim throughout. In case there was any question as to who's car this was originally, the factory installed a small plaque at the base of the steering wheel reading, "SH 10.13", SH for Sammy Hagar and 10.13 for his October 13th birthday. It should come as no surprise that the Ferrari also features a Harmon Kardon audio system to blast the tunes.

Delivered new to California and remaining there for all of Hagar's ownership, a new high-voltage lithium-ion battery was installed by Ferrari of San Francisco in January of 2024. Sold by Hagar in the fall of 2024 with 1,566 miles on the odometer, just 200 additional miles have been added in the ensuing two years for a total of 1,772 miles indicated at the time of cataloging.

If you can't drive 55 – and could easily be written up for doing 125 – than this one-off spec, bought-new by Sammy Hagar LaFerrari is sure to be the crown jewel of any collection.

THE TRUCK OFFERED

Inspired by the US Army's wartime 'Jeep', developed hastily and intended for short-term, small-scale production, the Land Rover would defy its creators' initial skepticism. Rover saw the need for a tough, four-wheel-drive, utility vehicle to serve the needs of the agricultural community in the immediately post-war years, but the Land Rover's runaway success took the company by surprise. The necessity of using corrosion resistant aluminum panels at a time of severe steel shortage became a positive virtue in the Land Rover's sphere of operations, and the use of existing components kept costs down and cut development time. Progressively developed since its launch in 1948 and modified to serve countless specialist requirements, the ubiquitous Land Rover looks set to continue well into the 21st Century.

The utilitarian Series III (and Defender that followed it) have bumped across the planet conquering trails and getting out of situations most trucks could not have gotten into in the first place. This aura has created a unique demand for Landys that retain the trucks rugged mystique while carefully uprating the machines aesthetically and mechanically for the modern era. Among the top marque specialists for the job are Ramble Rovers, whose exacting creations on the Defenders, Series, and Range Rover Classic platforms are hallmarks of what we all would have dreamed of coming from Sohilull factory.

This Series III 130 two-door was sourced from Portugal and stripped to the bare metal to be restored by Ramble Rovers. Had this been restored in the vein of their other commissions, it would have been a stellar machine – but this was taken a step further. Created as a Singular Work, the truck has been elevated from a vehicle to a rolling canvas – every square inch of the now-galvanized frame has been hand painted to reflect the unique spirit of Land Rover and Ramble Rovers outdoor heritage and global exploration. The stunning frame – revealing itself in the rear bumper and under the sills – sits beneath the carefully restored aluminum bodywork of the iconic machine. Finished in Diamond White, it is accented with galvanized folding windscreen and hoop set along with LED headlights, taillights, and turn signals. The interior is trimmed in Camel leather with front fluted seats and center console and center facing benches the length of the bed. The top frame has been further partially wrapped in leather and supports a newly trimmed tan top with tinted plastic side curtains. The ruggedness of the original vehicle is smoothed with a leather wrapped dashpad both top and bottom, a leather wrapped steering wheel, and white accent trim where black plastic would have formerly appeared. The floormats have been replaced with Carmel leather piped brown German square weave carpets and the vinyl door and tailgate cards have been refinished in matching tan leather.

Mechanically, the Wildlife Edition has been uprated with improved suspension, hydraulic ram power steering, a RoamerDrive SS Overdrive unit, and Black Wolf style rims shroud in massive BF Goodrich All Terrain TA KO2 tires.

Almost too stunning to get dirty, it is still a capable machine ready to attack Moab—or Indian Creek. Whether on the beach in the Hamptons, the Concours Lawn in California, or covered in mud on a grouse hunt, it is all but guaranteed to be the most stunning Land Rover around and a singular opportunity to own this amazing machine.

FERRARI F512 M

Introduced in 1994, the F512M was the final development of Ferrari's sensational Testarossa supercar. Ferrari's flagship model, the Testarossa revived a famous name from the Italian company's past when it arrived in 1984. A 'next generation' Berlinetta Boxer, the Testarossa retained its predecessor's amidships-mounted, 5.0-liter, flat-12 engine, the latter now boasting a maximum power output raised to 380bhp at 6,300rpm courtesy of four-valve cylinder heads. Despite the power increase, smoothness and drivability were enhanced, the car possessing excellent top gear flexibility contributing to a maximum speed of 180mph.

Rivalling Lamborghini's Countach for presence, the Pininfarina-designed Testarossa succeeded brilliantly, the gill slats feeding air to its side-mounted radiators being one of the modern era's most instantly recognizable – and copied - styling devices. A larger car than the 512BB - the increase in width being necessary to accommodate wider tires - the Testarossa managed the trick of combining high downforce with a low coefficient of drag, its graceful body being notable for the absence of extraneous spoilers and other such devices. Despite the increase in size over the 512BB, the Testarossa was lighter than its predecessor, the body - its steel doors and roof excepted - being, somewhat unusually for a production Ferrari, of aluminum. Luxury touches in the well-equipped cabin included air conditioning, electrically adjustable seats, tilting steering wheel and plentiful leather.

Unlike some of its rivals, the Testarossa possessed light controls and was relatively easy to drive, factors which contributed to its outstanding performance and stunning looks, contributed to an instant and sustained high level of demand. In 1992 the original Testarossa was succeeded by the updated 512TR version, which came with 428bhp on tap, while ABS brakes were added to the package before the 512TR was replaced by what would be the Testarossa's final incarnation – the F512 M – for 1995. For the first time there were major cosmetic changes: the original pop-up headlights being replaced by fixed lamps beneath clear covers, the grille size reduced, round tail lamps adopted and three-piece wheels fitted. Titanium connecting rods went into the engine, which produced marginally more power and torque than before. Only 501 examples of the F512 M had been completed when production ceased in 1996.

FERRARI 550 MARANELLO

With the introduction of the 550 Maranello in 1997, Ferrari returned to its tradition of building front-engined V12 sports cars, resurrecting a line that had remained dormant since the demise of the 365GTB/4 'Daytona' in 1974. The heart of any Ferrari is its engine, and the 550 Maranello's 48-valve, 5.5-liter V12 developed 478hp at 7,000rpm, some 100-or-so horsepower more than the Daytona's. Ferrari had discovered long ago that providing optimum balance in a front-engined sports car necessitated the use of a rear transaxle, and Maranello's came with six speeds. The power train was housed in a tubular steel chassis, to which was attached aluminum coachwork, while the all-independent suspension incorporated dual-mode (normal/sports) damping, switch-selectable by the driver, which was complemented by speed-sensitive power-assisted steering.

Styled by Pininfarina like its illustrious 'Daytona' predecessor, the 550 Maranello was similarly proportioned, adopting the classical combination of long bonnet, small cabin and truncated tail. The body's aerodynamics were developed in the wind tunnel, where hours of testing ensured that the minimum drag was combined with constant downforce regardless of set up, an important consideration in a 200mph road car. Styling details such as the bonnet air scoop and hot air outlets behind the front wheelarches recalled the great competition Ferraris of the past, in particular the immortal 250GTO, while the tail incorporated Ferrari's characteristic twin circular lights.

In 2004, Evo magazine published a 'Greatest Driver's Cars' feature that pitted the 550 Maranello against the Porsche 911 GT3, Honda NSX-R and Pagani Zonda C12S. The Ferrari won. "As with all great cars, there's no one facet that dominates the experience," declared the respected British motoring journal. "Yes, the engine is mighty, but the chassis is its equal. There's never been a supercar that's so exploitable and so rounded in its capabilities."

Finished in elegant Grigio Titanio over Dark Blue leather, the interior is further enhanced by Daytona-style seats, a 250 GT–inspired "diamond-stitched" headliner and rear shelf, along with rare carbon fiber trim. Notably, the cabin presents exceptionally well and is free from the commonly encountered "sticky" switchgear often associated with Ferrari's.

At its heart lies Ferrari's celebrated front-mounted V12 engine, further complemented by a Tubi Style exhaust system that delivers a more engaging and evocative soundtrack. The car is also optioned with optional 18-inch modular wheels, showcasing red-painted Ferrari brake calipers and completing its purposeful yet refined stance.

Accompanying the car are multiple keys, tools, a car cover, owner's manuals, the original build sheet, service records, and a battery tender.

Showing just 32,049 miles at the time of cataloging, this front-engined V12 grand tourer—paired with a highly desirable 6-speed manual transmission—offers a compelling opportunity for enthusiasts and collectors alike and stands poised as a modern classic within the Ferrari lineage.

As the market continues to favor analog, front-engined V12 Ferraris, the 550 Maranello has firmly established itself as one of the most important modern classics of its era. Final-year examples, particularly those offered in elegant color combinations with rare options, are increasingly sought after and tightly held. With limited availability and growing collector demand, this example represents an opportunity that is unlikely to be repeated in the near term—one that will appeal equally to the discerning collector and the enthusiast seeking one of the last truly engaging Ferrari grand tourers.

THE F12TDF

Introduced to the motoring public at the 2012 Geneva Motor Show, the Ferrari F12 replaced the 599 family of front-engined Gran Turismos. Evo magazine declared:

"The company has thrown everything at it to ensure it's vastly quicker than its seminal predecessor, but also that it's more enjoyable at low speeds. It claims to be both GT and supercar, mixing front-engined packaging and civility with exotic, F1-inspired dynamic ability."

Ferrari's gorgeous new Berlinetta was soon garnering critical accolades, being voted "Supercar of the Year 2012" by Top Gear magazine. Furthermore, in 2014 it received the coveted "Premio Compasso d'Oro ADI," one of the world's oldest and most prestigious design awards.

It is an oft-stated cliché that "the heart of every Ferrari is its engine." and the F12's 6.3-liter, 65-degree, normally aspirated V12 is acknowledged as one of the finest ever, winning the "Best Performance" and "Best Engine above 4.0-liters" categories in the 2013 "International Engine of the Year Awards." With 730bhp on tap, this class-leading power unit—one of the most powerful every installed in a Ferrari road car—delivers stupendous performance, propelling the F12 to 100km/h (62mph) in 3.1 seconds on its way to a top speed of 211mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, the F12 proved to be 3.5 seconds quicker that the preceding 599 GTB and 2.0 seconds quicker than the mid-engined Enzo. Even the hardcore 599 GTO was slower.

But these days even a supercar has to make the odd concession in the interests of fuel economy, and with this in mind, the F12 incorporated Ferrari's HELE stop/start system that reduces consumption when idling. Paddle shifters mounted on the steering wheel—an innovation pioneered by Ferrari in Formula 1—had long been a feature of the Maranello marque's road cars, and the F12's controlled a seven-speed dual-clutch semi-automatic transmission. Stability, traction control, suspension, and other settings were also controlled from the F12's steering wheel, while improved carbon-ceramic brakes helped keep things in check.

The engine/transmission package was mounted in an aluminum spaceframe chassis—developed by Ferrari's close neighbors and long-time collaborators, Carrozzeria Scaglietti—that represented significant gains in rigidity and weight reduction when compared with the preceding 599 GTB. As one would expect of a modern-day Ferrari supercar, the F12 came with the latest in driver aids as standard: ABS, SCM-E magnetorheological suspension, electronic limited-slip differential, ESP Premium stability control, and F1-Trac traction control.

Styled by the Ferrari Styling Centre and Carrozzeria Pininfarina, the F12's voluptuous body restated the traditional "long bonnet, small cabin, short tail" look in a manner suggesting muscular horsepower, while retaining all the elegance associated with the Italian coachbuilder's work for Maranello. A significant aerodynamic development was the "Aero Bridge": an under-body air channel running from front to rear that increased down force while exerting less drag than an external wing. Moreover, "Active Brake Cooling" ducts had been adopted for the same reason, opening only when the brakes required cooling while remaining closed at other times to reduce aerodynamic drag. The result was a remarkably low-drag coefficient of only 0.299. Based on that of the Ferrari FF, the "Frau leather" interior featured aluminum, Alutex, and carbon fiber trim. The F12's optional accessories were extensive, though pricey. Who would have thought that a carbon fiber cup holder could cost £2,112?

In October 2015, Ferrari announced a limited-edition variant, the F12tdf. Its nomenclature referencing a competition variant of the 250 GT, so named following the latter's many victories in the "Tour de France Automobile" in the late 1950s/early 1960s. Like its illustrious predecessor, the F12tdf was a lightweight, track-focused model aimed at wealthy connoisseurs and gentleman racers; only 799 were built during the 2016 and 2017 seasons.

The F12tdf used the same 6.3-liter V12 engine as the standard car, albeit modified to produce 769bhp, while deleting much of the leather/aluminum interior trim in favor of Alcantara and carbon fiber. Together, with swapping many exterior aluminum panels for carbon fiber, this helped shed some 110kgs from the total weight. The result was a reduction of the 0-100km/h to 2.9 seconds while the claimed top speed was now "in excess of 211mph." Around Fiorano, the F12tdf was 2.0 seconds quicker than its standard sibling.


THE CAR OFFERED

Unlike any other F12tdf, this example presented here is the product of Ferrari's own Tailor-Made program instead of a standard configurator ordered example. An exclusive service which goes beyond the regular exterior and interior options, those looking to personalize their vehicle even further, for a cost, can affect nearly every detail. Finished in the special-order exterior paint color Rosso TRS, it is accented with Nero DS stripes. Effectively every carbon fiber detail of the car has been finished in an exposed carbon look, even down to the engine cover and door cards in contrasting gloss and matte finishes. The wonderfully appointed interior is fitted with large size carbon fiber racing seats finished in perforated Nero Alcantara with Rosso stitched accents and a central Rosso leather strip. Affixed onto the car is a personalization specifications plaque listing every last custom treatment and it is recommended that one view this as to fully grasp the scope of the personalization. All in, the value of a nicely sized home was spent to achieve the final vision of the Ferrari's owner. Commissioned by a true Ferrari enthusiast and successful Corse Clienti driver, it joined a garage replete with a 550 Barchetta, 599GTO, Monza SP1, and more. According to the accompanying Yellow Book, this F12tdf was delivered to Ferrari of North America in October of 2016 and to the first owner by Ferrari of Newport Beach the next month with 62 'delivery' miles. The first eight years of the car's life were spent in Orange County being regularly serviced by the Ferrari of Newport Beach, as affirmed by the clean CARFAX report. Currently, the odometer shows only 335 miles, and the tdf appears as close to 'as new' condition as a 'preowned car' can get.

The F12tdf is truly a modern-day collectible that will continue to be held in high esteem by collectors and enthusiasts alike. With one of the classiest looking color combinations, this vehicle is sure to catch the eyes of most passerby. This F12tdf is surely one of the most well thought-out and desirable builds to leave Maranello. As such, the sale of this beautifully sculpted limited production supercar presents and incredible opportunity that should not be missed.

THE FERRARI DINO 246 GT

The Dino, a name that has captured imaginations with its elegance and technical sophistication, stands as one of Ferrari's most beloved models. Conceived as a tribute to Enzo Ferrari's late son, Alfredo "Dino" Ferrari, the series was to bring refined mid-engine performance to a wider audience. Announced at the 1965 Paris Motor Show as a Pininfarina-penned dream, the production Dino 206 GT launched in 1968 and soon evolved into the more potent 246 GT by 1969. The latter brought with it essential revisions: a larger V-6, a steel body for added durability, improved power, and slightly extended dimensions, all while preserving the siren-like handling that defined the original design.

At its core, the 246 GT is powered by the intriguing 2.4-liter V-6 engine, initially developed for Formula 2 racing. Featuring a 65-degree aluminum block with dual overhead camshafts and fed by triple Weber carburetors, the engine produced a distinctly melodic, high-revving soundtrack synonymous with Ferrari's racing lineage. Mated to a close-ratio five-speed gearbox and riding on a rigid, well-balanced steel chassis, the Dino delivered one of the most intuitive and rewarding driving experiences of its era.

Pininfarina's coachwork evolved gracefully from the angular lines of the early 206 to the sensual curvaceous form of the 246 GT, blending compact elegance with aerodynamic prowess. The new steel construction ensured the Dino's lasting presence in the collector world, while the adoption of wider Campagnolo wheels and larger disc brakes improved both handling and stopping power. These advancements laid the groundwork for Ferrari's later mid-engine road cars, marking the Dino as a formative model in Maranello's history.

The 246 GT was also significant for Ferrari's burgeoning presence in the vital American market. US-specification models, such as the example offered here, were equipped with additional safety features, revised lighting, and emissions controls in order to meet stringent Federal standards of the era. Though subtle in appearance, these details further distinguish the rare US-market Dinos in the eyes of astute collectors.

Original color combinations play a significant role in the appeal of a Dino, and the beguiling Rosso Dino—a vivid orange-red hue introduced in period—remains among the most coveted and rare. The contrast of Rosso Dino with the Nero (black) leather interior is an especially evocative pairing, highlighting both the car's Italian flamboyance and modernist, purposeful interior architecture.

Throughout its production from 1969-1974, fewer than 2,500 Dino 246 GTs were produced, with numbers for well-preserved and highly original examples exceptionally low today. The Dino's combination of design purity, driving enjoyment, and Ferrari heritage has ensured its lasting desirability, and original examples with documented provenance are among the most sought-after of all Maranello road cars.

Collector interest has grown steadily in recent decades, elevated by the Dino's intrinsic beauty, rewarding road manners, and its position at the confluence of two legendary automotive houses: Ferrari and Pininfarina. Prime, unrestored examples are increasingly regarded as reference standards, offering unique appeal to purists and aficionados alike.

Today, the Dino 246 GT is recognized not only as a cornerstone of Ferrari road car development, but as a superlative sports car in its own right—celebrated for its character, engineering sophistication, and undeniable charm.


THE CAR OFFERED

The Dino 246 GT presented here, chassis number 03752, occupies a place of particular distinction. Completed in 1972 for the United States market, it was delivered new through famed North American importer Chinetti Motors—an origin detail cherished by knowledgeable marque enthusiasts.

Verified by detailed provenance and factory documentation, this car retains its original, matching-numbers V-6 engine (no. 135 CS 000 0009506) and five-speed manual transmission (type 888 E), as documented by factory records.

Immediately striking is the car's exceptionally rare and desirable color combination: Rosso Dino (20-R-350), a vibrant, period-correct orange-red, over Nero VM8500 leather. This alluring specification, seldom seen on US-delivered cars, accentuates both the Dino's lithe proportions and its high-style 1970s Italian heritage. The car retains its original glass and a highly original interior, displaying a remarkable level of preservation seldom encountered among Dinos of this provenance.

A single high-quality repaint was executed in the original Rosso Dino, carefully preserving the factory appearance while refreshing the car's unmistakable visual allure. The interior, including seats, door panels, and dashboard, believed to be unrestored in original Nero VM8500 leather. This balance of diligent cosmetic stewardship and preservation demonstrates the meticulous care this car has received throughout its life.

Under long-term private ownership since its acquisition on January 6, 2000, the current owner has maintained the car in well preserved condition. The Dino shows 24,568 miles at the time of cataloguing, a figure reported to be original.

Additionally, the car is accompanied by original accessories, including its set of original keys, owners' manuals, factory tool roll, and a period workshop manual for the model, as well as Ferrari technical documentation the 'Dino Compendium'.

It's a rare and factory-correct color specification, sparingly documented mileage, and single-owner provenance for over two decades make it a standout among its peers—a ready candidate for preservation awards, concours exhibition, or continued enjoyment as a reference-standard example of Ferrari's formative mid-engine masterpiece.

For the astute collector, chassis 03752 presents an opportunity to acquire a truly authentic, highly original Dino 246 GT.

The Chiron's foundation is its extraordinary 8.0-liter quad-turbocharged W16 engine, a mechanical marvel producing a staggering 1,578 horsepower in Super Sport trim. Inside, the Chiron cocoons occupants in a sybaritic environment, marrying old-world craftsmanship with cutting-edge technology. Fine leathers, machined metals, and carbon-fiber elements abound; all tailored to customer specification. Every detail, from switchgear to seat embroidery, exudes the exclusivity expected of the Bugatti badge.

Drawing inspiration from Bugatti's "300+" world-speed record car, the Super Sport features a lengthened and refined aero package, unleashing prodigious speed while ensuring day-to-day usability. Across the globe, the Chiron has been celebrated at concours events, featured in prestigious collections, and lauded by the world's top automotive journalists. Its rarity—less than 500 were planned across all Chiron variants—underscores its immediate status as a collectible investment.

Owning a Chiron, particularly in Super Sport configuration, marks entry into a rarefied echelon of automotive connoisseurs. The model's blend of technical innovation, bespoke craftsmanship, and unrelenting performance personifies the Bugatti legacy in the twenty-first century. THE MEYERS MANX

In the 1960s, the fiberglass kit-car craze was taking hold in America. Versatile and inexpensive, fiberglass was easy for the average enthusiast to use, and custom car builders, racers, and hot-rodders turned to it as a viable alternative to sheet metal to turn their dreams into reality. Able to be molded into any shape imaginable, fiberglass build-your-own car kits sprang up to suit an endless variety of donor cars.

The most distinctive car of the genre emerged from the California workshops of Bruce F. Meyers. Mr. Meyers was an engineer, boat builder, artist, tinkerer, surfer, and amateur desert racer who sparked the kit-car craze of the 60s. Eschewing the typical sports car and "Kustom" styles favored by other kit manufacturers, Meyers designed and built a VW Beetle-based machine that was equally at home on the beach, the street, or racing through the desert – the original Dune Buggy. Drawing from his boat building experience, Meyers created the first dune buggy using a shortened VW drivetrain fitted to fiberglass monocoque body with a mix of VW and Chevy truck suspension parts. He named it the "Manx" after the stubby, short-tailed Manx cat.

Donor Beetles were cheap, plentiful, and readily tunable which gave the light and nimble Manx astonishing performance both on and off-road. Bruce Meyers' little buggy first made headlines in 1967 when it set the four-wheel Baja Peninsula speed record, and then again when it won the 1967 Mexican 1000 desert race (the predecessor to the Baja 1000), proving its mettle as a serious competition car. Sales exploded and soon scores of copies began flooding the market as the dune buggy craze took off. However, the copycats never captured the magic of the original Meyers Manx, which remained in production for years, and is now a bona fide cult-classic, and authentic Meyers originals continue to be prized by enthusiasts worldwide. In 2019, Bruce Meyers Meyers, who passed his legendary brand on to the current caretakers in 2019, launching a new Meyers Manx to carry on his legacy.

While the collection is retaining a handful of other special buggies, it is time for "Surfs Ep" to go to new caretakers where it can continue to deliver more smiles per mile.

Developing an imposing 647 horsepower at 6,250 rpm, it channels power through a lightning-quick seven-speed Getrag dual-clutch transmission, launching the GT from rest to 60 mph in just over three seconds. Not merely a powerhouse, this engine is also a marvel of efficiency and responsiveness, honed through Ford's intensive experience with turbocharged endurance racing technology.

Every detail of the GT's underpinnings reflects a racing intelligence rarely seen on road cars. The suspension represents a formula-level innovation, with active damping and ride height adjustment contributing to both daily comfort and track domination. Carbon-ceramic disc brakes provide immense, fade-free stopping power, while advanced active aerodynamics—including an adaptive rear wing and deployable flaps—ensure optimal stability at any speed.

Despite its rarity and technical pedigree, the GT is more than a mere showpiece: it is an unequivocally driver-centric supercar. Collectors and connoisseurs have flocked to the model, not simply for its inherent exclusivity—limited to just 1,350 builds across its production span—but for its historical significance as a true analogue to Ford's modern racing conquests.

Rarity, purpose, and provenance combine to ensure the Ford GT's revered status among the world's foremost collectors. Delivering superlative road manners and sonorous performance, the S/T stands as a dynamic showcase of what is possible when tradition and innovation are blended with discipline and pride. Within this Ultimate Series contains some of the most potent and exclusive cars to be released from McLaren. This includes the familiar names like the P1, Senna, Senna GTR, Speedtail and finally the latest iteration of their ultimate offering, the venerable Elva.

The McLaren Elva depicts this ultimate driving emotion where the F1 had left off many years ago. McLaren had set out to build a vehicle so powerful, so lightweight and delivering a completely different driving experience than any of their other vehicles offered. To do this, a drastic approach would need to be taken to achieve status of giving a driver the driving experience from a whole new world. This drastic approach includes eliminating the entire roof, windows and windscreen. Couple that with copious amounts of lightweight carbon fiber body panels as well as the carbon chassis, a highly advanced aerodynamic body design and a superbly responsive 804 horsepower twin turbocharged V8 engine; this completes the recipe for an astounding experience in a road car. Performance from this lightweight and powerful machine comes with astounding numbers including an estimated 0-60 time of 2.8 seconds while 0-124mph is stated to take an astonishing 6.7 seconds. Top speed on this roadster is claimed to hit 203 mph. The Elva was the machine that McLaren developed to mimic what a modern day Can-Am racecar would be like today. Truly an amazing driving experience.

The Elva is the lightest modern production road car that McLaren has ever produced. Although they have yet to announce its actual weight, the writing is on the wall considering the amount of high-tech, lightweight composite details used on this car. The Elva is equipped with a bespoke carbon fiber monocoque which is mated to a full carbon fiber body which is comprised from only three main panels. The front carbon fiber clamshell is stated to be only 1.2mm in thickness proving how minimalistic their approach was to achieving extreme lightness. Most of the interior is adorned by carbon fiber as well as the unique carbon fiber seats clad in a new synthetic 'Ultrafabric' material to help the occupants stay firmly gripped into the seats. THE FORD GT

Unveiled at the 2002 North American International Auto Show as a rolling tribute to Henry Ford II's Le Mans-conquering GT40s, the Ford GT was conceived as an audacious celebration of both the brand's centennial and its competition prowess. Its gestation reflected the finest in American motorsport legend—a modern reinterpretation of the iconic GT40, shaped via advanced computational design yet informed by the demands of road and track.

Developed by Ford's Special Vehicle Team (SVT) under the direction of Camilo Pardo and Chris Theodore, the GT promised breathtaking performance harnessed within an instantly recognizable silhouette. Every styling detail—the sloping roofline, the gaping hood nostrils, the low-slung haunches—evoked the mythos of the 1960s original. Automotive enthusiasts immediately recognized the GT not merely as a retro exercise, but as a bona fide supercar, intended to stand shoulder to shoulder with Europe's best.

Engineered around an aluminum spaceframe chassis and clothed in superformed aluminum panels, the Ford GT exemplified meticulous construction. At its heart lay a 5.4-liter, all-aluminum, double overhead cam V8, augmented with an Eaton twin-screw supercharger and robust internals. This formidable powerplant yielded an official output of 550 horsepower and 500 lb-ft of torque—figures that, even today, demand respect. Crucially, a Ricardo-sourced six-speed manual gearbox, renowned for its mechanical precision, fed the rear wheels, offering an unfiltered connection between driver, engine, and tarmac.

Technically, the GT left little to be desired. In addition to its formidable straight-line pace—0 to 60 mph in under 3.5 seconds, and a top speed cresting 200 mph—the chassis was a masterclass in balance. Four-wheel independent suspension, Brembo monobloc brakes, and bespoke Goodyear Eagle F1 Supercar tires delivered composure and poise required at the highest echelon. In the realm of analog supercars, few machines ever rivaled its holistic blend of speed, handling, and mechanical tactility.

Inside, Ford's flagship spared no expense: Ebony leather, magnesium switchgear, and exposed aluminum surfaces evoked both racecar function and modern luxury. The ergonomics spoke to a purity of mission—minor concessions for comfort, maximum focus upon the driver's engagement. Among connoisseurs, subtle differences in color, options, and "stripe delete" configurations have become coveted markers of rarity among the already scarce production run.

Manufactured at Ford's historic Wixom Assembly Plant in Michigan, only 4,038 Ford GTs were completed between 2004 and 2006. Final-year cars, such as the example offered, benefited from production refinements and—due to limited build slots—heightened exclusivity. Of those, an even smaller fraction were allotted to export markets, equipped to comply with local regulations and fitted with metric instrumentation.

Today, the Ford GT is widely admired as a canonical American supercar—collectible, exhilarating, and faithfully evocative of one of motorsport's greatest legacies. Preserved, low-mileage, and scarce-specification cars remain on the shortlist for enthusiasts, museum curators, and blue-chip collectors seeking superlative provenance and show-stopping performance in a single, timeless package.

A rare, low-mileage, and highly original Ford GT in one of the model's most desirable configurations, chassis 402008 represents a compelling opportunity for the discerning collector.
