THE BUGATTI VEYRON

To say that the Bugatti Veyron caused a sensation when it arrived in 2005 would be a gross understatement; for here was a car that didn't just rewrite the supercar rule book so much as tear it up and start afresh. All the more remarkable was the fact that the Veyron was the dream of one man: Ferdinand Piech, CEO of the Volkswagen Group, which had acquired the Bugatti brand in 1998. Piech's ambition was to create a car that had 1,000 horsepower at its disposal, could exceed 400km/h (250mph), and cost €1 million. Turning Piech's dream into a reality would prove to be an immensely difficult undertaking, even for a company with Volkswagen's technological resources, and the result would not see the light of day for another seven years.

Designed by ItalDesign boss Giorgetto Giugiaro, the first concept car – the EB118 – was displayed at the Paris Auto Show in 1998, featuring permanent four-wheel drive and a Volkswagen-designed W18 engine. A handful of variations on the theme were displayed at international motor shows over the course of the next few years before the concept finally crystallized in 2000 in the form of the Veyron EB 16.4. The latter was styled in house at VW by Hartmut Warkuß and featured an engine with 16 cylinders and four turbochargers – hence the '16.4' designation. It was named after Bugatti development engineer and racing driver, Pierre Veyron, who together with co-driver Jean-Pierre Wimille, had won the 1939 Le Mans 24-Hour race for the French manufacturer. But this was far from the end of the development process, and it would take another five years and an extensive shake-up of the project's management and engineering teams before production could begin, by which time an incredible 95% of components had been either changed or redesigned.

Effectively two narrow-angle 4.0-liter V8 engines sharing a common crankcase, the 8.0-liter W16 - just - met Piech's requirements, producing a maximum output of 1,001bhp and 922ft/lb of torque, figures that would embarrass a current Formula 1 car. With a curb weight of 1,888kg (4,162lb) the Veyron had a staggering power-to-eight ratio of 523bhp per ton. Tasked with transmitting this formidable force to the ground was a permanent four-wheel-drive, dual-clutch transmission system incorporating a seven-speed paddle-shift semi-automatic gearbox, the latter built by the British company, Ricardo, while to accommodate the Veyron's phenomenal top speed Michelin designed special run-flat PAX tires. Piech had specified a maximum velocity of 250mph, and the Veyron did not disappoint, with more than one tester – Top Gear's James May included - exceeding the target by a few miles per hour. At $1,250,000 (€1,225,000) the Veyron base price as also exceeded Piech's target comfortably.

To maintain stability at such high speeds, the Veyron has a few aerodynamic tricks up its sleeve, a hydraulic system lowering the car at around 140mph, at which speed the rear wing deploys, increasing downforce. But if the Veyron driver wishes to exceed 213mph (343km/h), he or she needs to select Top Speed Mode (from rest) before joining what is a very exclusive club indeed.

Jeremy Clarkson, reviewing the Veyron for The Times: "In a drag race you could let the McLaren (F1) get to 120mph before setting off in the Veyron. And you'd still get to 200mph first. The Bugatti is way, way faster than anything else the roads have seen." Yet despite its breathtaking performance, the Veyron contrived to be surprisingly docile at 'sensible' speeds. "Bugatti says the Veyron is as easy to drive as a Bentley, and they're not exaggerating," declared Autocar. "Immediately you notice how smoothly weighted the steering is, and how calm the ride is."

In a market sector many of whose protagonists can only be described a 'hard core', the Veyron contrived to be a remarkably civilized conveyance. "When you climb aboard the Bugatti Veyron there are no particular physical contortions required of you by the world's fastest car, as there are in so many so-called supercars," observed Autocar describing "the most exquisite car cabin on earth". The latter was found to be more than generously spacious for a two-seat mid-engined car, while in terms of interior equipment there was virtually no limit to what the, necessarily wealthy, Veyron customer could specify. Restricted rearward visibility is a frequent bugbear of mid-engined supercars, a problem the Veyron dealt with by means of a reversing camera.

In 2009, an open version of the Veyron – the Grand Sport – was announced, featuring a removable roof panel and 'emergency' soft-top. The following year Bugatti released the ultimate Veyron - the Super Sport - which came with 1,200bhp, 1,100ft/lb of torque, and revised aerodynamics. Only 30 were made, the very last of these truly fabulous cars being that offered here. An open version - the Grand Sport Vitesse - was introduced in 2012.

The SSC Ultimate Aero had taken the Veyron's title of 'World's Fastest Car' in 2007, but the Super Sport would soon put the upstart American manufacturer in its place. The redoubtable James May achieved a top speed of 259.49mph (417.61km/h) on 4th July 2010, and later that same day Bugatti test driver Pierre Henri Raphanel set a new mean best mark of 267.856mph (431.072km/h) at Volkswagen's test track near Wolfsburg in Germany. This had been achieved by deactivating the Super Sport's electronic limiter, which restricts top speed to 'only' 258mph (415km/h), causing some to question the figure's validity. Eventually, the Guinness Book of Records decided that the mark should stand. By the time Veyron production ceased in 2015, Bugatti had built only 450 of these quite extraordinary cars.


THE CAR OFFERED

One of just 178 Veyron 16.4 Coupes built and a mere 76 manufactured to US specification, '150' was completed at the factory in Molsheim, France in November of 2007 and delivered new in December of that year to its first owner near San Diego, California. Finished in Italian Red with Gloss Black accents over an interior richly trimmed in Red and Black Alcantara, this French road rocket spent much of its life between California, Florida, and the Michigan.

Regularly driven and enjoyed, it is a rare example of a modern hypercar that has gathered several hundred miles under tire each year. In the ensuing years, the Bugatti has received a full paint protection film by Tier1autohaus in Las Vegas, Nevada as well as a custom titanium exhaust system from Ryft.Co – reducing the weight of the exhaust from 42 pounds to only 9 pounds while giving the car an even more sonorous soundtrack – and Ryft.Co forged black wheels. It should be noted that a February 24, 2012 'damage report' is listed on the CARFAX (but the report does not indicate any details, uncommon for a CARFAX report) – but this is contradicted by the AutoCheck report that indicates no accidents or damage reported.

Showing 12,645 miles from new at the time of cataloging, this missile from the verdant hills of Alsace is ready to move onto its next, lucky owner. Complete with owner's handbooks, CARFAX, AutoCheck, face-melting speed, physics-defying acceleration, and unmatched luxury are just a bid away.

THE PORSCHE 911 CARRERA S (993)

By the end of the 20th century, the Porsche 911 had become an undoubted automotive icon—its evocative form, distinctive rear-engine layout, and the relentless pursuit of driving excellence shaping generation after generation of enthusiast and collector. The fourth and final iteration of the air-cooled 911, internally codenamed the 993, entered production in 1994 and bowed gracefully in 1998, closing the air-cooled era with technical sophistication, potency, and balance unmatched by its predecessors.

The 993 Carrera S stands at the pinnacle of this celebrated lineage. Introduced in 1997 and offered in limited quantities through the conclusion of 993 production, the Carrera S mated the wide-body 'Turbo-look' chassis with the Carrera's naturally aspirated flat-six powerplant, creating a rare and charismatic combination prized by collectors today. Its muscular stance, lower ride height, and distinctive split-grille engine cover separated the S from its narrower brethren. Only a fraction of total 993 production left the factory as Carrera S models, making each example highly sought after.

Underpinning the Carrera S's allure are its technical advancements. The M64/23 engine delivered a potent 282 horsepower in stock form, its air-cooled architecture refined to an art form: traction control, a sophisticated multi-link rear suspension, and six-speed transmission all contributed to remarkable roadholding and tactility. The Carrera S was more than cosmetic—a finely honed driver's machine, balancing robust performance with everyday usability.

The 993's robust construction and purity of purpose earned it laurels not only in period reviews but also enduring admiration among marque devotees. Famed for its composure at speed, its unfiltered steering, and its extraordinary reliability, the 993 generation endures as a true sweet spot for drivers who crave classic Porsche spirit, imbued with just enough modernity.

As Porsche's last air-cooled series, the 993 enjoys lasting cachet—particularly in its Carrera S guise, which, with its Turbo-width hips and rarity, occupies a unique space between the more common Carrera and the high-powered Turbo. These models are at once subtle and muscular, focused yet approachable, and always an event to experience.

Recent years have seen a global resurgence in customized Porsche culture, epitomized by the Renngesellschaft Werkbau (RWB, or "RAUH-Welt Begriff") movement. Fusing Japanese tuning artistry with German engineering foundation, RWB conversions have swept concours lawns and magazine pages alike, celebrated for their extravagantly flared arches, radical stance, and bespoke interiors. Each RWB build is individually commissioned and personally assembled by the founder, Akira Nakai, whose signature on the dashboard denotes authenticity—and cult status.

For the discerning Porsche aficionado or collector, an RWB-converted Carrera S is the ultimate synthesis: a rare, numbers-matching platform that harmonizes factory engineering brilliance with international tuning artistry. The result is an exclusive and highly individualized 911, combining revered mechanical genes with unconstrained visual impact.


THE CAR OFFERED

This striking 1998 Porsche 911 Carrera S presents a rare opportunity for the collector seeking the hard-to-find convergence of Porsche originality and RWB artistry. Completed in Stuttgart on December 4, 1997, this vehicle began life as a Canadian market car, specified with the desirable M64/23 engine and 6-speed manual transmission.

Originally finished in Arctic Silver Metallic with a Savanna Beige leather interior, this Carrera S has since undergone a visually and technically transformative journey to become the first QC-commissioned RWB Porsche in Canada. Now resplendent in British Racing Green—expertly applied to highlight the wide-shouldered silhouette unique to the S—the car wears the hallmarks of Akira Nakai's celebrated handwork, signified by his "QC 1" signature on the dashboard. This designation alone marks the car as a pivotal RWB creation: not simply an RWB, but the first Canadian RWB based on the rare Carrera S chassis, rather than on the far more commonly modified narrow body Carrera or Carrera 4 variants.

Every aspect of this build exemplifies the merging of performance ambition with meticulous execution. The exterior is dominated by bespoke RWB fenders and signature aero, complemented by RWB wheels, brakes, and distinctive headlamp treatments. The cockpit has been entirely reimagined, eschewing its original configuration for a full suite of high-performance and luxury materials: swathes of Alcantara envelop the dashboard, headliner, door sills, and rear shelf (converted to a purposeful rear compartment). The seats are embossed with RWB branding, paired to carbon fiber door panels and a color-matched roll b, creating an environment at once purposeful and visually arresting.

Modernization and performance are equally prioritized: a CAE ultra-precise shifter, Porsche Classic radio, backup camera, and Focal sound system fuse contemporary convenience with enthusiast sensibility. The instrument cluster and steering wheel, both modified in the RWB tradition, complete the transformation. Mechanically, the car has been significantly upgraded with a Protomotive turbo kit, delivering a dramatic increase in power and torque over factory specification. The multi-piece Work wheels are wrapped with Toyo R888R tires to provide race-bred grip fit for the car's enhanced performance envelope; the entire chassis and suspension remain true to Porsche's vaunted geometry, ensuring a balance of roadgoing stability and track-readiness.

Serving as a testament to its robust build and the reliability of its restored and upgraded state, this car displays 145,748 kilometers—clear evidence of both sustained enjoyment and mechanical longevity. Its numbers-matching engine and transmission further reinforce its collectability, a crucial factor given the Carrera S platform's rarity among RWB builds.

This 1998 Porsche 911 Carrera S RWB "QC 1" is an irresistibly rare fusion of air-cooled Porsche collectability and the avant-garde, coachbuilt RWB ethos. The execution and quality of its mechanical and aesthetic upgrades, combined with its unrepeatable status as the first Canadian S-based RWB, render it a truly peerless offering—a centerpiece for any discerning Porsche or bespoke motorcar collection.

THE FERRARI DINO 246 GTS

In the vibrant tapestry of Ferrari history, the Dino occupies an especially prized and lyrical niche. Conceived in honor of Enzo Ferrari's late son, Alfredo "Dino" Ferrari, the 246 series marked a significant departure for Maranello. It was the marque's first mid-engined, six-cylinder road car—an eloquent bridge between motorsport and the open road, named not Ferrari, but simply "Dino," suggesting both reverence and a sense of evolving identity.

Launched in 1969, the Dino 246 GT captured the imagination of enthusiasts and the public alike, blending Ferrari's commitment to mechanical excellence with shapely, Pininfarina-penned coachwork by Scaglietti. The 246 GTS, unveiled in 1972, built on this legacy, introducing a targa-style variant that added a new dimension of open-air motoring while preserving the coupe's distinctive proportions. With its removable roof panel, "GTS" offered an intoxicating union of Supercar drama and the sunshine of la dolce vita.

At the heart of every 246 beats the revered 2.4-liter dual overhead cam V-6, derived from Formula 2 roots and characterized by responsive power delivery and thrilling aural character. Triple Weber 40 DCNF carburetors, alongside a 5-speed dogleg manual transmission, imbue the car with an unmistakable sense of mechanical connection—supple and tractable enough for daily use, but transcendent at the redline.

Chassis sophistication was equally advanced, with an all-independent suspension and four-wheel disc brakes—features that gave the Dino surprising agility and composure. Lightweight and balanced, the 246 quickly earned a reputation for purity of handling; its steering and throttle response remain benchmarks for driver involvement.

The Dino's coachwork, with its curvaceous flanks and delicate details, is widely regarded as one of Pininfarina's masterpieces. Interior appointments were no less considered—the laid-back driving position, aircraft-inspired Veglia instrumentation, and available Daytona-style seats made each journey an event.

Originally intended to challenge rivals like the Porsche 911S, the Dino instead carved out its own cult following. Only 1,274 GTS models were built between 1972 and 1974; a mere fraction were finished in rare metallics and special-order paint schemes (like Marrone Dino Metallizzato), marking such examples as true connoisseur's prizes today.

In the decades since production ended, the Dino's reputation has matured immeasurably. Where it was once an "almost-Ferrari," it is now recognized as one of the marque's most poetic and influential creations. The GTS models, in particular, capture an era of playful, unrestrained artistry in both mechanical design and visual language.

Chassis 05496 represents a singular opportunity: an exceptionally well-documented and lovingly preserved 1973 Ferrari Dino 246 GTS, ordered and retained in its original, highly coveted Marrone Dino Metallizzato (106-M-73) finish over beige leather (VM3218).

Built on April 19, 1973, this E Series U.S.-specification Dino is notably one of only 215 examples delivered in this evocative livery—a color that imbues the timeless Pininfarina bodywork with depth, elegance, and a warm period authenticity rarely encountered.

The car's provenance is both rich and meticulously maintained. Delivered new through legendary importer Chinetti Garthwaite Import Inc., it was first sold to Don Fong's Inc. in Atlanta, Georgia. Its ownership chain is exceptionally well-attested, traced through prominent collectors and enthusiast caretakers in Texas, Connecticut, Mississippi, California, Florida, Ohio, and Montreal, each contributing to a continuous narrative of use, preservation, and service. This unbroken chain is verified by a trove of archival documents, including service invoices and repair orders spanning nearly half a century—among them, rare period entries from Simpson Automobili (Houston, 1976), Eurocar Werk (1978), and Woodard's World of Wheels (1979).

Beyond its provenance, 05496 stands as a model of originality. The car retains its original, numbers-matching 2.4-liter V-6 engine (no. 1966 E) and 5-speed manual gearbox—both confirmed by an authoritative certified archival summary performed by Dino expert Matthias Bartz in June 2024.

Benefitting from consistent preservation-minded ownership, the car now shows just 52,500 miles from new—a figure substantiated by successive service and repair records as well as state and dealer registrations. In addition to noteworthy authenticity, 05496 was specified with highly desirable factory options when new, including the iconic Daytona seats, power windows, and air conditioning.

In 2000, the significance of its preservation was formally recognized, earning both Best in Show and Platinum Award honors at the Lime Rock Ferrari Club of America meet—a testament to the car's presentation and correctness amid the highest standards of the Ferrari judging community.

In 2024, the Dino was entrusted to marque specialists for a comprehensive mechanical and cosmetic recommissioning totaling over $45,000. This included a complete windows-out repaint in its factory-original shade, painstaking repairs to the radiator and underbody, and the installation of fresh rubber seals for the removable top. The dash was reupholstered using correct "mouse hair" material, ensuring period texture and appearance. Additional work encompassed a new oil pressure sender, correct exhaust hanger, aluminum back plate level holder, fresh battery, and thermostat, while the carburetors were tuned to perfection. Upon reassembly, the car received a full wet-sand and detailed polishing, leaving the presentation both dazzling and authentic.

Throughout its life, 05496 has always been maintained with diligence, as attested by the original tool kit, jack, keys, manuals, warranty documents, and over four decades of maintenance records—all of which accompany the sale. The Dino Compendium's Certificate of Authenticity further confers peace of mind regarding the car's identity and mechanical fidelity.

This Dino exemplifies the ideal collector's paradigm: rare, dazzlingly original, exceptionally well-documented, and ready for both spirited touring and the concours lawn. With its intoxicating color, pure mechanical specification, comprehensive provenance, with only over 52,500 original miles, chassis 05496 stands not merely as a fine Ferrari, but as an irreplaceable chapter in the story of the Dino marque.

Here is an invitation to experience one of Maranello's most lyrical creations—preserved, cherished, and poised for its next custodian.

MERCEDES-BENZ 280 SE 3.5 CABRIOLET

In the pantheon of postwar luxury automobiles, few models command the reverence, and admiration accorded the Mercedes-Benz W111-series Cabriolet, and none more so than the potent and lavishly appointed 280 SE 3.5. Introduced in late 1969, the 3.5-liter variant marked the ultimate evolution of the prestigious W111 platform, at once marrying Mercedes-Benz's storied engineering prowess with newfound V8 performance and subtle, old-world elegance.

Conceived at a time when Mercedes-Benz sought to reaffirm its leadership within the realm of open Grand Tourers, the 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet combined the sweeping, pillarless silhouette of the original Paul Bracq-penned design with significant mechanical advancements. At its heart lay the M116 V8: a single-overhead-cam, all-alloy motor of 3,499 cubic centimeters, breathing through sophisticated Bosch D-Jetronic electronic fuel injection. This combination yielded an exhilarating 200bhp, a figure that transformed the W111 Cabriolet from stately tourer to swift express, fully capable of sustained Autobahn velocities.

Hand-assembled in limited numbers at the legendary Sindelfingen works, the 3.5 Cabriolet was a singular accomplishment, blending robust German engineering with the finest materials available. The opulent interiors featured exotic wood veneers, hand-stitched leather, and finely chromed hardware—details emblematic of Mercedes-Benz's uncompromising standard of craftsmanship. Furthermore, the model's fully independent suspension and four-wheel disc brakes complemented the powerful V8, ensuring dynamic poise and refined composure on both sweeping highways and sinuous country roads.

The exclusivity of the 3.5 Cabriolet was defined not only by its performance or luxury, but also by its scarcity. Just 1,232 Cabriolets were produced between 1969 and 1971, and fewer still were delivered to original European specification. Today, their desirability persists, with discerning collectors coveting unrestored examples or those returned to as-new condition by the world's foremost specialists.

The 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet enjoys an exalted reputation amongst Mercedes-Benz connoisseurs, owing to its place as the final hand-built, open-top model of the classic era. It stands as Mercedes-Benz's swan song to a world before mass production altered the automotive landscape—a graceful, V8-powered masterwork embodying both the manufacturer's technical acumen and its dedication to understated elegance.

In period, the 3.5 Cabriolet was the preferred conveyance of captains of industry, film stars, and heads of state, offering unparalleled comfort and performance in equal measure. Its effortless road manners, ample power reserves, and whisper-quiet operation set a benchmark that rivals and successors would struggle to attain.

Further elevating its appeal is the car's ability to blend discreet luxury with subtle aggression. At a glance, the casual observer might miss the discreet "3.5" badging and low, wide grille—further emphasizing its status as a sophisticated grand tourer for those who value substance over ostentation.

Today, the W111 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet stands at the zenith of postwar Mercedes-Benz collector interest, cherished for its rarity, integrity, and fully realized synthesis of performance and grace. The finest examples—those retaining their original mechanicals and finished in compelling color schemes—are considered blue-chip investments within the international collector community.

THE PORSCHE 911 (993) CABRIOLET

In 1993 Porsche introduced what is regarded by many as the most beautiful 911 of them all: the Type 993. Over the years the 911's purity had been diluted by various safety add-ons. The Type 993 marked a return to basics, being recognizably a 911 but freed of extraneous bits to spoil its lines. Beneath the beautiful body, engineers devised a new light-alloy sub frame with an all-new multi-link suspension, putting behind the previous generations' lift-off oversteer and making significant progress with handling and refinement. The 993 was also the first 911 to receive a six-speed transmission, and engines gained variable intake and sophisticated modern electronic management. The range comprised of two- and four-wheel drive models, the legendary Turbo, and the Cabriolet convertible, all powered by the latest, 3.6-liter version of Porsche's perennial air-cooled flat-six engine.
